grammar.x: In English, sentence order NEVER changes: Subject first, then Verb, then Object. Unlike Spanish, you cannot move the object before the subject. This is the single most important rule — if you get this right, you will be understood even with mistakes elsewhere.

ok.e: I need the report.
ok.t: Necesito el reporte.

ok.e: She sent the email yesterday.
ok.t: Ella envió el email ayer.

ok.e: They finished the project on time.
ok.t: Terminaron el proyecto a tiempo.

no.w: Subject first: I need
Object never goes first in statements

grammar.t: #2 — To Be: Two Spanish Verbs in One
grammar.s: I am / You are / He-She-It is
grammar.x: English uses ONE verb ('to be') where Spanish uses TWO ('ser' and 'estar'). Memorize the conjugation: I AM, you/we/they ARE, he/she/it IS. Never combine 'to be' with another verb that isn't -ING form. 'I am agree' is WRONG because 'agree' is already a verb.
grammar.f: I am | You/We/They are | He/She/It is

ok.e: I am ready for the meeting.
ok.t: Estoy listo para la reunión.

ok.e: She is a senior analyst at Google.
ok.t: Es analista senior en Google.

ok.e: They are working on the migration.
ok.t: Están trabajando en la migración.

no.w: Drop 'am': I have a question

no.t: She is agree with the plan.
no.w: 'Agree' is a verb: She agrees

grammar.x: This is the #1 mistake Spanish speakers make. In present simple, when the subject is he/she/it (third person singular), you MUST add -S to the verb. I work → She workS. I write → He writeS. Rules: consonant+y → -ies (study→studies), -sh/-ch/-x/-o → -es (go→goes, watch→watches). This rule ONLY applies to present simple affirmative.

ok.e: She writes SQL queries daily.
ok.t: Escribe queries SQL a diario.

ok.e: He manages the entire data pipeline.
ok.t: Él administra todo el pipeline.

ok.e: The script runs every morning at 6 AM.
ok.t: El script corre cada mañana a las 6.

no.w: She workS from home
He DOESN'T like meetings

grammar.x: Spanish negation is simple: put 'no' before the verb. English is different — you need an auxiliary. I/You/We/They + DON'T + base verb. He/She/It + DOESN'T + base verb (NO -S on the main verb!). Past tense: DIDN'T + base verb for ALL subjects. The main verb stays in base form after don't/doesn't/didn't.

ok.e: I don't have the file yet.
ok.t: No tengo el archivo aún.

ok.e: She doesn't work on Fridays.
ok.t: Ella no trabaja los viernes.

ok.e: We didn't finish the report.
ok.t: No terminamos el reporte.

no.w: I DON'T have the file
Base form after doesn't: work (no -S)

grammar.s: Do / Does / Can / Will + Subject + Verb
grammar.x: In English, you CANNOT make a question just by changing intonation (unlike Spanish). You need an auxiliary verb at the beginning. Do/Does for present, Did for past, Will for future, Can/Could for ability/requests. After the auxiliary, use the BASE form of the verb (no -S, no -ED). With 'to be', invert: 'You are ready' → 'Are you ready?'

ok.e: Do you have experience with Python?
ok.t: ¿Tienes experiencia con Python?

ok.e: Can you send the file by tomorrow?
ok.t: ¿Puedes enviar el archivo para mañana?

ok.e: Did she finish the analysis?
ok.t: ¿Ella terminó el análisis?

no.w: DO you have experience?
Does she WORK here? (base form)

grammar.x: Use past simple for completed actions with a specific time. Regular verbs add -ED (worked, created, analyzed). Irregular verbs change form entirely — you MUST memorize them. Key irregulars: go→went, build→built, make→made, see→saw, have→had, do→did, get→got, take→took, find→found, write→wrote, speak→spoke, give→gave, run→ran, come→came, think→thought, send→sent, know→knew, say→said.

ok.e: I created a dashboard that saved 20 hours per week.
ok.t: Creé un dashboard que ahorró 20 horas/semana.

ok.e: We built an automated pipeline in Q3.
ok.t: Construimos un pipeline automatizado en Q3.

ok.e: She found a critical bug in the data.
ok.t: Ella encontró un bug crítico en los datos.

no.w: Irregular: I BUILT the pipeline
Irregular: She WENT to the meeting

grammar.x: Use this for actions happening RIGHT NOW or temporary projects in progress. Structure: subject + am/is/are + verb-ING. You MUST include the auxiliary 'to be' — 'I working' is WRONG. Also used for planned future actions: 'I am presenting tomorrow.' Do NOT use with state verbs (know, want, need, like, believe, understand) — say 'I know' not 'I am knowing.'

ok.e: I am working on the churn analysis right now.
ok.t: Estoy trabajando en el análisis de churn ahora.

ok.e: We are migrating the database to Snowflake.
ok.t: Estamos migrando la base de datos.

ok.e: She is presenting the results tomorrow.
ok.t: Ella presenta los resultados mañana.

no.w: I AM working on it (need auxiliary)
State verb: I KNOW the answer

grammar.x: Both express future, but with nuance. WILL: spontaneous decisions, promises, predictions ('I'll send it now'). GOING TO: planned intentions, evidence-based predictions ('I'm going to present on Friday'). After WILL, use base form — NEVER 'to'. In conversation, they're often interchangeable. Contraction: I will → I'll, we will → we'll.
grammar.f: Subject + will / am going to + verb (base form)

ok.e: I will send the report tonight.
ok.t: Enviaré el reporte esta noche.

ok.e: I am going to present at the standup tomorrow.
ok.t: Voy a presentar en el standup mañana.

ok.e: We'll fix the bug before the release.
ok.t: Arreglaremos el bug antes del release.

no.w: No 'to' after will: I will send
Base form: She will SEND

grammar.x: Use present perfect for experience, achievements, and actions with no specific time. 'I have worked with Python for 3 years' (still relevant now). Key signal words: ever, never, already, yet, for, since, recently, just. If you mention a SPECIFIC date, switch to past simple: 'I worked there in 2022' (NOT 'I have worked'). Has = he/she/it. Have = I/you/we/they.

ok.e: I have worked with Python for 3 years.
ok.t: He trabajado con Python por 3 años.

ok.e: She has led multiple cross-functional projects.
ok.t: Ha liderado múltiples proyectos.

ok.e: We have already deployed the fix.
ok.t: Ya desplegamos la corrección.

no.w: Past participle: I have WORKED
Specific date → past simple: I worked there in 2022

grammar.x: For real, possible future situations. The IF clause uses present simple (NEVER will), and the result clause uses WILL + base verb. You can swap the order: 'We will save time if we automate.' This is the conditional you'll use most in business: 'If we launch early, we'll capture more market share.'
grammar.f: If + present simple, subject + will + base verb

ok.e: If we automate this process, we will save 10 hours.
ok.t: Si automatizamos este proceso, ahorraremos 10 horas.

ok.e: If the data is clean, the model will be accurate.
ok.t: Si los datos están limpios, el modelo será preciso.

no.w: No 'will' in the IF clause: If we automate...

grammar.x: Modal verbs express ability, possibility, advice, or polite requests. CAN = ability/permission ('I can write SQL'). COULD = polite request or past ability ('Could you review this?'). SHOULD = advice/recommendation ('You should validate the data'). WOULD = hypothetical or polite preference ('I would recommend BigQuery'). After ALL modals: base verb only. No 'to', no -S, no -ING.

ok.e: I can write complex SQL queries.
ok.t: Puedo escribir queries SQL complejas.

ok.e: Could you review my pull request?
ok.t: ¿Podrías revisar mi pull request?

ok.e: We should schedule a meeting.
ok.t: Deberíamos agendar una reunión.

ok.e: I would recommend using Python for this.
ok.t: Recomendaría usar Python para esto.

no.w: No 'to': I can write SQL
Base form: She can WRITE code

grammar.t: #12 — Passive Voice: Focus on the Action
grammar.x: Use passive voice when the action matters more than who did it. Very common in reports and technical writing. 'The data was cleaned' (we don't care who did it). 'Metrics are tracked in real time.' Form: subject + to be (conjugated) + past participle. To mention the doer, add 'by': 'The report was created by the analytics team.'
grammar.f: Object (becomes subject) + to be + past participle

ok.e: The data was cleaned and validated.
ok.t: Los datos fueron limpiados y validados.

ok.e: Metrics are tracked in real time.
ok.t: Las métricas se rastrean en tiempo real.

ok.e: The report will be shared by Friday.
ok.t: El reporte será compartido para el viernes.

no.t: The data was clean by the team.
no.w: Past participle: was CLEANED by the team

grammar.s: The most missed words by Spanish speakers
grammar.x: Articles are tiny but critical. A/AN = one non-specific item (a report, an error). THE = specific item both speaker and listener know (the report I sent you). ZERO article = general categories or uncountable nouns (Data is important. People are diverse.). Use AN before vowel SOUNDS (an hour, an SQL query) not just vowel letters (a university, a European).
grammar.f: a/an = non-specific | the = specific | Ø = general/uncountable

ok.e: I found an error in the dataset.
ok.t: Encontré un error en el dataset.

ok.e: The meeting is at 3 PM.
ok.t: La reunión es a las 3.

ok.e: Data is the new oil.
ok.t: Los datos son el nuevo petróleo. (general = no article)

no.w: Uncountable: I need information (no article)
Superlative needs THE: She is THE best analyst

grammar.x: To compare two things: short adjectives (1-2 syllables) add -ER + than (faster than, bigger than). Long adjectives (3+ syllables) use MORE + than (more efficient than). For superlatives (the best of all): short → THE + -EST (the fastest), long → THE MOST (the most important). Irregulars: good→better→best, bad→worse→worst, far→farther→farthest.
grammar.f: A is adj+er / more adj than B | A is the adj+est / the most adj

ok.e: Python is faster than Excel for large datasets.
ok.t: Python es más rápido que Excel para datasets grandes.

ok.e: This is the most efficient pipeline we've built.
ok.t: Este es el pipeline más eficiente que hemos construido.

ok.e: My SQL skills are better than last year.
ok.t: Mis habilidades SQL son mejores que el año pasado.

no.t: Python is more faster than Excel.
no.w: Never double: Python is FASTER (not more faster)

no.t: This is the most good solution.
no.w: Irregular: the BEST solution

grammar.x: Some verbs are followed by -ING (gerund): enjoy, avoid, consider, finish, mind, keep, suggest, recommend, practice. Others by TO + verb (infinitive): want, need, decide, plan, hope, agree, expect, offer, refuse, learn. Some accept both with no change: like, love, hate, start, begin, continue. Some change meaning: 'stop smoking' (quit) vs 'stop to smoke' (pause to do it).

ok.e: I enjoy working with data.
ok.t: Disfruto trabajar con datos.

ok.e: I decided to learn Python.
ok.t: Decidí aprender Python.

ok.e: We need to consider changing the approach.
ok.t: Necesitamos considerar cambiar el enfoque.

no.t: I enjoy to work with data.
no.w: Enjoy + ING: I enjoy WORKING
Decide + TO: I decided TO LEARN

grammar.x: Relative clauses add information about a noun. WHO = people ('The analyst who built the dashboard'). WHICH = things ('The report which was sent yesterday'). THAT = both, in defining clauses ('The tool that we use'). WHERE = places ('The team where I worked'). WHOSE = possession ('The client whose data was lost'). In informal English, THAT often replaces WHO/WHICH.

ok.e: The analyst who built this dashboard is on my team.
ok.t: El analista que construyó este dashboard está en mi equipo.

ok.e: The tool that we use for ETL is Airflow.
ok.t: La herramienta que usamos para ETL es Airflow.

ok.e: The company where I worked had 500 employees.
ok.t: La empresa donde trabajé tenía 500 empleados.

no.w: People → WHO: The analyst WHO built this
Things → THAT/WHICH: The tool that we use

grammar.s: If + past simple → would + base verb
grammar.x: Use for imaginary or unlikely situations in the present/future. 'If I had more time, I would learn R.' The past simple in the IF clause does NOT mean past time — it signals unreality. WOULD + base verb in the result. Special: with 'to be', use WERE for all subjects in formal English: 'If I were you, I would...' (not 'was'). Common in interviews: 'What would you do if...?'
grammar.f: If + past simple, subject + would + base verb

ok.e: If I had more time, I would learn machine learning.
ok.t: Si tuviera más tiempo, aprendería ML.

ok.e: If we were a bigger team, we would split the work.
ok.t: Si fuéramos un equipo más grande, dividiríamos el trabajo.

no.t: If I would have more time...
no.w: No 'would' in IF clause: If I HAD more time

grammar.x: Phrasal verbs combine a simple verb with a preposition to create a completely new meaning. They are EVERYWHERE in business English. You cannot guess the meaning from the individual words. 'Look up' ≠ mirar arriba (it means buscar/investigar). 'Figure out' ≠ figurar fuera (it means descifrar). Master these 10 and you'll sound much more natural.

ok.e: I need to figure out why the query is slow.
ok.t: Necesito descifrar por qué el query es lento.

ok.e: Can you set up the development environment?
ok.t: ¿Puedes configurar el entorno de desarrollo?

ok.e: Let me break down the numbers for you.
ok.t: Déjame desglosar los números.

ok.e: We need to follow up on the client's request.
ok.t: Necesitamos dar seguimiento al pedido del cliente.

no.t: I need to out figure this.
no.w: Don't split: figure OUT (or figure this out)

no.t: Can you up set the server?
no.w: Correct order: set UP the server

grammar.x: When reporting what someone said, the verb tense shifts back (backshift). Present → Past: 'I work here' → She said she worked there. Past → Past Perfect: 'I finished' → He said he had finished. Will → Would: 'I will send it' → She said she would send it. Can → Could. For questions: 'Do you...?' → She asked if/whether I... No question mark in reported questions.

ok.e: She said she would send the report by Friday.
ok.t: Dijo que enviaría el reporte para el viernes.

ok.e: He told me he had already finished the analysis.
ok.t: Me dijo que ya había terminado el análisis.

ok.e: They asked if we could join the meeting.
ok.t: Preguntaron si podíamos unirnos a la reunión.

no.t: She said she will send it.
no.w: Backshift will→would: She said she WOULD send it

no.t: He asked do I have the file?
no.w: No question form: He asked IF I had the file

grammar.s: Things you did regularly but no longer do
grammar.x: USED TO + base verb: past habits or states that are no longer true. 'I used to work in accounting' (but now I'm in data). WOULD + base verb: repeated past actions only (NOT states). 'I would always double-check the numbers.' You CANNOT say 'I would be an accountant' for a past state — use 'used to' for states. Negative: 'I didn't use to...' (no D). Question: 'Did you use to...?'
grammar.f: Subject + used to / would + base verb

ok.e: I used to work in accounting before switching to data.
ok.t: Solía trabajar en contabilidad antes de pasar a datos.

ok.e: We would always review the data before presentations.
ok.t: Siempre revisábamos los datos antes de presentaciones.

no.w: Past form: I USED to work there
States need 'used to': I USED TO BE an accountant

m.t: Hey! How is it going?
Pretty good, thanks! Busy week though.
Same here. Lots of deadlines.
Yeah, I've been swamped with the migration project.
m.r: Sí, he estado saturado con la migración.

m.t: Let's go around. Miguel, what's your update?
Yesterday I finished the churn analysis dashboard.
m.r: Ayer terminé el dashboard de análisis de churn.

m.t: Today I'll focus on validating the Q3 metrics.
m.r: Hoy me enfocaré en validar las métricas de Q3.

m.t: Any blockers?
I need access to the production database. Could you approve that?
m.r: Necesito acceso a la base de producción.

v: Today I'll focus on... = Hoy me enfocaré en...

m.t: Welcome! Table for how many?
Two, please.
Can I get you something to drink?
I'll have a water, please.
Ready to order?
I'll have the chicken pasta. That's all, thanks!
m.r: La pasta con pollo. ¡Eso es todo!

m.t: Thanks for coming in. Tell me a little about yourself.
m.r: Gracias por venir. Cuéntame un poco de ti.

m.t: Sure! I'm a data analyst with 3 years of experience in SQL, Python, and Tableau.
m.r: Claro, soy analista de datos con 3 años de experiencia.

m.t: What attracted you to this role?
I'm excited about the opportunity to work with large-scale datasets and drive business decisions through data.
m.r: Me emociona la oportunidad de trabajar con datasets grandes.

m.t: Great. What's your greatest strength?
I'd say it's my ability to translate complex data into clear, actionable insights for non-technical stakeholders.
m.r: Diría que es mi habilidad para traducir datos complejos en insights claros.

v: Tell me about yourself = Cuéntame de ti
What attracted you to...? = ¿Qué te atrajo de...?
I'd say it's... = Diría que es...

m.t: May I speak with Miguel?
Speaking! How can I help?
Could you send the Q3 report by end of day?
m.r: ¿Podrías enviar el reporte de Q3 hoy?

m.t: Absolutely. I'll have it to you by 5 PM.
m.r: Por supuesto. Te lo envío a las 5.

v: By end of day = Para hoy / antes de terminar el día
I'll have it to you by... = Te lo envío para las...

m.t: How was your weekend?
Great! I went hiking and practiced some Python.
m.r: ¡Genial! Fui de excursión y practiqué Python.

m.t: Nice! I just binge-watched a series on Netflix.
m.r: ¡Bien! Yo vi una serie completa en Netflix.

m.t: Sounds relaxing! Which one?

v: How was your weekend? = ¿Cómo estuvo tu finde?

exercises.q: She said she _____ send the report by Friday.

exercises.q: Traduce: Necesito el reporte para mañana.

al: I need the report for tomorrow.

exercises.q: Traduce: ¿Puedes enviarme el archivo?

al: I'm working on a new project.

exercises.q: Traduce: Ella no trabaja los viernes.
exercises.a: She does not work on Fridays.

exercises.q: Traduce: El analista que construyó el dashboard es de mi equipo.
exercises.a: The analyst who built the dashboard is on my team.
al: The analyst that built the dashboard is on my team.
exercises.w: Relative clause: WHO for people. Built = irregular past.

exercises.q: Traduce: Ella dijo que enviaría el reporte el viernes.
exercises.a: She said she would send the report on Friday.
al: She said that she would send the report on Friday.

behavioral.m: I am a data analyst with experience in SQL, Python, and Tableau. I specialize in turning raw data into actionable insights. In my previous role, I built automated dashboards that saved 15 hours per week for the operations team.

I'd say it's my ability to translate complex data into clear stories for non-technical stakeholders. For example, I presented a customer segmentation analysis to the C-suite that led to a targeted campaign, resulting in 20% higher retention.
t: Give a specific example with numbers

behavioral.q: Tell me about a time you failed.
behavioral.m: Early in my career, I built a dashboard without validating the source data. A wrong business decision was made based on it. I took full ownership, corrected the data, rebuilt the dashboard with automated validation checks, and presented the corrected insights. Now data quality is my strongest area.

I combine strong technical skills in SQL, Python, and visualization tools with genuine business acumen. What sets me apart is my ability to connect data insights directly to business outcomes that impact revenue and efficiency.

technical.q: What tools do you use for data analysis?
technical.m: My core stack is SQL for data extraction and transformation, Python with pandas and scikit-learn for analysis and modeling, and Tableau for visualization. I also work with BigQuery, Git for version control, and I'm currently learning dbt for data transformation.

technical.q: How do you handle messy data?
technical.m: I follow a systematic approach. First, I assess the extent of the issues — missing values, duplicates, inconsistent formats. Then I investigate root causes with the data engineering team. I document every cleaning decision for transparency and reproducibility, and I always validate the cleaned data against known business rules.

situational.q: How do you handle multiple urgent requests?
situational.m: I assess each request by business impact and deadline, then communicate clearly with all stakeholders about realistic timelines. I deliver quick wins where possible while working deeper analyses in parallel. If I truly can't handle everything, I escalate early rather than delivering late.

situational.q: What would you do if you found an error in a shared report?
situational.m: I would immediately notify all stakeholders who received the report, clearly explain the error and its impact, correct the data, send the updated version with a summary of changes, and implement automated validation to prevent recurrence.

hispanicErrors.why: Age uses TO BE, not TO HAVE
'Agree' is already a verb — no 'to be' needed
-ED = how you feel, -ING = what causes the feeling
Use can't / cannot, never 'no' before modals
The preposition is always ON, not OF

strategies.title: Don't translate word by word
strategies.desc: Capture the general idea. Understanding 60% of a sentence is enough to follow the conversation.

strategies.title: Listen for STRESSED words
strategies.desc: In 'I NEED the REPORT by FRIDAY', the capitalized words carry the meaning. Function words are swallowed.

strategies.title: Ask them to repeat — no shame
strategies.desc: 'Could you repeat that?' or 'Sorry, I didn't catch that.' Native speakers expect this.

strategies.title: English subtitles (not Spanish!)
strategies.desc: Watch YouTube or Netflix with English subtitles. 30 minutes per day. Your brain links sound to text.

strategies.title: Shadowing technique
strategies.desc: Repeat what you hear 1 second later, imitating intonation and rhythm. Best exercise for pronunciation.
